hook: A diver tumbles off a platform, arms and legs flying in every direction, yet one point of her body traces a smooth arc into the pool. A thrown wrench spins wildly but one point glides in a straight line. Physics finds that point, the center of mass, and lets you treat a whole messy object as a single dot.

prereq.q: In the object model, an object is treated as
options: a single point with a position
a point with a size and shape
a set of separate moving parts
prereq.why: The object model keeps only a position: no size, shape or inner parts.

prereq.q: A projectile's path, with air ignored, is
prereq.why: Constant velocity sideways plus constant acceleration downward gives a parabola.

figure.caption: The center of mass sits nearer the heavier ball; a system is whatever you draw the boundary around.

chain.cause: You draw a boundary around the objects you care about
chain.effect: they form the system, and everything else is the surroundings

chain.cause: The parts of the system are not what the question is about
chain.effect: you can model the whole system as one point object

chain.cause: The system's mass is not spread evenly
chain.effect: that point, the center of mass, sits nearer the heavier parts: x_cm = Σm·x ÷ Σm

chain.cause: The system moves, tumbles or turns
chain.effect: its center of mass still moves like a single point object, so you can track one point instead of every part

ideas: A system is the object or objects you choose to study; everything outside the boundary is the surroundings.
Mass is a scalar measure of how much matter there is, in kilograms; masses add.
The center of mass is the mass-weighted average position: x_cm = (m₁x₁ + m₂x₂ + …) ÷ (m₁ + m₂ + …). Do x and y separately.
For a uniform, symmetric object the center of mass is on every line of symmetry. It can be in empty space (a ring).

misconception.wrong: The center of mass is halfway between the objects, or at the middle of the object.
misconception.right: Only for equal masses or a uniform object. Otherwise weight each position by its mass: the center of mass is closer to the heavier part.

summary: Choose a system and its boundary; when its insides do not matter, model it as one point at its center of mass, the mass-weighted average position x_cm = Σm·x ÷ Σm, which lies nearer the heavier parts and on any line of symmetry.
